subject: principles-of-accounts
title: Absorption and Marginal Costing: Where the Fixed Overhead Goes

segments.say: Both unit costs build from the same three variable layers. Direct materials $10, direct labour $6 and variable production overhead $4 land in both columns, layer by layer, giving $20. Point at the two unit costs on your student notes before the fixed overhead arrives.
questions: Which three layers land in both unit costs?
What is the variable cost of one unit, and how is it built?

segments.say: Fixed overhead lands only in the absorption column. The $12,000 spread over 1,000 units is $12 per unit, taking absorption to $32, while marginal costing sends the whole $12,000 to the period. Now try the unit-cost questions on your worksheet.
questions: Why is the absorption unit cost $32 but the marginal unit cost $20?
Where does the $12,000 go under marginal costing?

segments.say: Closing inventory carries $2,400 of fixed overhead forward. Only 800 of the 1,000 units are sold, so 200 units sit in inventory holding $12 each under absorption costing. Check the deferral against your student notes before moving on.
questions: How many units are in closing inventory?
How is the $2,400 carried forward calculated?

segments.say: Absorption profit is higher by exactly that $2,400. Marginal profit is $7,000, absorption profit is $9,400, and the gap is the deferral and nothing else. Keep the two unit costs, the 200 unsold units and the $2,400 deferral in view as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
questions: What are the two profit figures?
What single amount reconciles them, and where does it sit?
segments.watchFor: Absorption and marginal costing always report the same profit, because fixed production overhead is a period cost under both methods. Listen for students who say the method cannot change profit, or who expense the fixed overhead under both methods. Send them back to scene 3 and the closing inventory: The methods differ on timing: marginal costing expenses the full $12,000 of fixed production overhead in the period, but absorption costing attaches $12 per unit to inventory, so the 200 unsold units carry 200 x $12 = $2,400 of fixed overhead forward in closing inventory - which is why absorption profit of $9,400 exceeds marginal profit of $7,000 by exactly that $2,400 deferral.
